paras: Thank you for this morning. Below are the next steps, so that both sides are working from the same plan rather than from two different memories of the same call.

We are meeting on the fourth of March for the kick-off, and that date is already in both calendars. The handover from our commercial team to delivery happens in the same week, and Flavio stays on the project until the first steering group, so that nothing is lost between the two teams. Marta is going to name a project owner on the Harbrook side before the kick-off; that decision was taken last week and only the name is missing.

One line is not ours. The firewall change on your side has a six-week lead time, and it is the only item on this plan that nothing will remind anybody about. If it is requested in the first week of March, everything after it holds. If it is requested in April, the pilot moves and go-live moves with it.

The pilot starts on the sixth of April with two customers and runs for one month. Onboarding for the wider team follows immediately after. Go-live is the first of July, and there are two weeks of contingency inside that date, which we are writing down rather than hiding: if we use them, we will say so at the steering group. I will send the full plan tonight, and we can align on it in fifteen minutes on Thursday rather than by email.

items.situation: The kick-off is in both calendars for the fourth. Say it.
tips: We are meeting on the fourth of March.
In the calendar means the -ing form, not will.

items.situation: Their team decided last week to hire a project manager. Say it.
tips: They are going to hire a project manager.
Decided before this conversation means going to.

items.situation: You decide right now to send the plan tonight. Say it.
tips: I will send you the plan tonight.
Decided as you speak means will.

items.situation: The pilot has fixed dates in the plan. Say it.
tips: The pilot starts on the sixth of April and runs for one month.
A timetable takes the present simple, like a train.

items.situation: Name a six-week wait that belongs to the customer, without blaming them.
tips: The firewall change has a six-week lead time on your side, so it is on the plan from day one.
Name it as a plan item, not as a complaint.

items.situation: The customer has just said yes and the call is ending. Say the most valuable sentence.
tips: Shall we lock in the kick-off now, while everybody is here?
A date agreed later is a date that slips.

listenings.text: There is a gap after the yes that almost nobody plans for, and in most companies it is about three weeks long. Sales has finished, delivery has not started, and for those three weeks nobody actually owns the customer. The cure is one sentence, and it has to be said before the end of the call where they agree: shall we lock in the kick-off date now, while everybody is still in the room. A date agreed in the room happens. A date agreed later by email is a date that slips, and it slips quietly. The other thing I watch, and this is the one that breaks plans, is any lead time that belongs to the customer. A firewall change, a purchase order, a security review. Twenty minutes of work and six weeks of waiting, and nothing in anybody's system will remind them it exists. So it goes on the plan on day one, with their name on it, said out loud.

I will tell you what I actually judge a supplier by, and it is not the demo and it is not the price. It is the first two weeks after I sign, because those two weeks tell me what the next two years are going to look like. The most common thing that happens, and the thing I remember longest, is that the salesperson disappears. Somebody new arrives, they ask me questions I already answered twice, and I understand that the person I was really dealing with was selling and not delivering. And there is one more thing I want in writing, even when it is bad news. Tell me the contingency, and tell me the lead times that belong to my own side. I would much rather see two weeks of contingency written down in March than discover it in June. A plan that hides that is a plan that is going to surprise me, and I have had enough surprises.
